roles.criterion: what a perfect question or lesson has
roles.method: how to make or check one
roles.context: what bounds the others: limits, measures, research

facets.key: the right answer and its marking
facets.stimulus: the text, document or source a question rests on
facets.scoring-guide: the rubric or marking guide for written answers
facets.feedback: what a student is told after answering
facets.hints: help before the answer is given
facets.alignment: fit to the objective, unit and what was taught
facets.sequence: order and spacing across a lesson or course
facets.evaluation: judging content with a model or code
facets.measurement: how quality and learning are measured

stages.ground: fix the objective, the scope and the facts before writing
stages.write: draft the stimulus, question, options, guide and feedback
stages.settle: check in code everything code can decide
stages.judge: ask bounded questions of an independent judge
stages.review: people and scripted readers check what the judge can't
stages.measure: measure quality and learning the same way each time
stages.improve: fix causes, one change at a time

existing: A check that has never fired proves nothing until it catches a fault planted for it.
Use a judge to check a bounded claim, not to hunt for faults.
A lesson that passes every check is well formed, and a first-try answer shows the moment; whether anyone learned needs a later test on new items.
A question about a text must need the text.
Agreement between a judge's samples is consistency, not correctness, and its choices can shift with the order of the options.
Beside every judgment of a student's words, ask whether they are aimed at the marker rather than the task.
Accept a right answer nobody planned for, but only when the judge is sure, and log it for review.
Ask a question right after the part that answers it, make sure it needs that part, and never stop mid-sentence.
Give background at the line that needs it.
Captions word for word with the narration: they make a film usable without sound, but in one study text identical to the narration impaired learning.
Check what a machine made against something that doesn't assume the answer.
Check every generated or repainted picture by eye against its brief and the text, and draw maps and diagrams from data.
Quote exactly, and check every quotation against the text in code.
Feedback on a wrong answer says where to look, never what the student has to produce, and only what is true of what they were given.
Put few words on screen, the ones the voice is saying as it says them: in one study, two or three per slide helped retention.
Fix the scoring rule and the expected answers before measuring, apply them the same way to every option, and leave arguable cases out.
Gate every check: one a student can skip is decoration, so a seek past an unanswered question goes back to it.
Give a judge exactly what the student sees, one bounded question at a time.
A marker can apply a rubric's rule only if it is given what the rule refers to; otherwise enforce the rule in code.
Keep directions on how to read apart from the words to be read, and let them set only the tone: one voice model read its own instructions aloud.
Keep every judgment whole, so it can be replayed or re-asked of another judge; where two judges agree against an answer key, check the key.
Keep what students write and show it back; a model's confident reading can choose a hint or move on, but not give a grade.
Don't read liking as learning: in one study every kind of picture raised satisfaction, but only instructive ones raised recall.
Keep machine checks apart from human judgment: a quality call stays unjudged until a person has watched or listened, and an AI judge only picks what that person reviews.
Mark meaning, not wording: any wording that says it counts, a short answer can be enough, and a point made on an earlier try still counts.
Take every length and time from the delivered file, leave a value empty until it is measured, label an estimate as one, and stop the build rather than guess.
Don't adapt to a student on fewer than three observations.
Never ask a student to say or perform a line with a slur in it: a line a student performs ships only when a judge confirms it is clean.
Nothing a student sees or hears may give the answer before the first attempt, including the picture behind a paused question.
How to nudge a reader who stalls or keeps guessing; nothing in my engine does yet.
A choice question needs one answer the text settles; check the right option, and each wrong one, on its own.
Every line a student reads gets one plain voice: no praise, no exclamation marks, no verdict the screen already shows, and at most one question, none in a closing line.
With many candidates, ask one yes-or-no question about each and combine the answers in code.
Order a lesson: what students already know, the source, a worked example, guided tries, their own explanation, a check, and a later transfer.
Before a judged check holds back a lesson or steers a student, score it on cases a person labelled; a model-made label measures nothing.
A picture should show what the voice is saying.
Record where every asset came from and its hash, check the hash before using it, and treat a source note as a record of origin, not a licence to reuse.
Give every animated picture a reduced-motion version with the same information and a text description, and never let colour carry meaning alone.
When a rule changes, remake what was made under the old rule instead of serving it.
Report how students do skill by skill, on items that need the text.
Review a lesson in the mode students get: one player's reviewer mode let a seek skip its checks, and the students' mode never did.
Save the first attempt as well as the last: first-try answers are how two designs get compared.
Before a person sees a lesson, have scripted readers play it: one who knows, one who guesses, one who is stuck, and one who tries to game it.
Meet a length limit by splitting the material into parts, not by cutting or speeding up approved words.
Spread the right answer's position evenly across a set, and check it in code.
Stills or motion: in some studies still pictures with printed text teach as well as narrated animation, but across many, animation wins on average.
Test whatever marks an answer when the model is slow or down, because that path marks real students too.
Two blocks of one kind in a lesson must test different things; tell the writer what the earlier one covers.
Two tries, then the answer; otherwise a student who never gets it right can't finish.
An unsure judge has said neither yes nor no: unsure is never a pass and never a miss, the student keeps the answer, and a part the judge can't confirm is left out.
The same marker can give different verdicts on the same answer: send each test answer more than once, and re-send every known miss after each rebuild.
Who reads what students write, and what anyone learns from it, once their words are kept and never marked.
Point at a text by its words, never its line numbers: editions number lines differently, and a lesson may show none.
Teach and gloss the words that carry what a reader needs to know, not the rarest ones, each for its sense in its own line.
Let a model write only the free text a lesson needs, and make every choice, mark and check a bounded judgment that, at play time, picks among lines written and checked in advance.
